annotations.title: A New Radio to Overcome Critical Link Budgets
annotations.error_annotation: The error is that the beamforming gain for N antennas is incorrectly calculated as N, when it should actually be N^2, since coherent beamforming results in the received power increasing by the square of the number of antennas.

flags.location: Section III.A, paragraph after Eq. (4)
flags.description: Unitarity does not give the stated T-fold SINR improvement. A unitary row has squared norm 1, so matching it preserves white-noise variance and recovers h_n x_{b,n} without an integration gain. The unit-modulus tones in Eq. (7) instead have squared norm T and are not unitary-normalized; these two normalizations are conflated.
flags.evidence: The manuscript states: "If the matrix F_b is unitary" the matched filters "provide the T-fold improvement of SINR." Eq. (7) assigns unit-modulus complex exponentials to waveform samples.

flags.location: Section III.A, comparison following Eq. (3); numerical-results paragraph on temporal combining gains; abstract
flags.description: The comparison counts temporal integration as a replacement for transmit beamforming gain although the longer subcarrier symbols already consume that integration time. Set h_n=1, T=N, unit transmit amplitude, and sample-noise variance sigma^2. Eq. (1) gives beamforming SNR N^2/sigma^2 per symbol; Eq. (4) with orthogonal unit-modulus rows gives N/sigma^2 after matching. Both send N symbols in N samples with total transmit power N. Thus MA-TISK remains a factor N below beamforming in this equal-power, equal-throughput example.
flags.evidence: Following Eq. (3): "For T = N, the same combining gain as with transmit beamforming is achieved." The numerical results compare temporal gains of 12.6 and 12.2 dB to the 12.0 dB beamforming gain. The abstract concludes: "There is no loss in link budget gain compared to spatial beamforming at the transmitter."

flags.location: Subsection C, Transmit Beamforming vs. MA-TISK, opening paragraph
flags.description: The restriction of beamforming spatial multiplexing to the near field is false. In a far-field rich-scattering channel, two angularly resolvable paths can support two simultaneous transmit/receive beam pairs and two spatial streams. Narrow beams can select those paths; they do not necessarily reduce channel rank to one. The rank-one precoder in Eq. (1) describes a single-stream choice and does not establish this restriction on beamforming generally.
flags.evidence: The text asserts: "For transmit beamforming spatial multiplexing is only an option in the near-field." The preceding Spatial Multiplexing subsection instead identifies "near-field communication or rich scattering" as alternatives, and the manuscript explicitly discusses forming multiple beams for distinct propagation paths.

flags.location: Subsection C, Transmit Beamforming vs. MA-TISK; final paragraph on peak data rate
flags.description: The claimed linear growth of peak rate with SNR omits the finite spatial-rank limit of the fixed antenna array. Activating additional streams can trade surplus SNR for rate over a limited range, but once all available spatial modes are used, applying Eq. (9) to each mode gives a finite sum of logarithmic rate terms. The described reuse of existing antennas does not justify unrestricted linear rate growth with SNR.
flags.evidence: Subsection C says "MA-TISK can convert a linear increase in link-budget into a linear increase in data rate" by grouping pairs, quadruples, or 8-tuples of waveforms. The final claim is: "Peak data rate can be made to grow linearly with SNR by means of spatial multiplexing even in far field scenarios." Eq. (9) gives R = log_2(1 + SNR).

rows.title: A Relationship Between Nonphysical Quasi-probabilities and Nonlocality Objectivity

annotations.title: A Relationship Between Nonphysical Quasi-probabilities and Nonlocality Objectivity
annotations.error_annotation: The error is that the calculation incorrectly claims different eigenvalues for β^{T}β in the right-identity case, when in fact the eigenvalues remain unchanged for both the left- and right-identity cases, invalidating the argument's main result.

flags.location: Equations (8)–(9), Theorem 1.4, and its construction
flags.description: The matrix product for a single nonzero row is an outer product, not a diagonal matrix of squared entries. Consequently, qubit swapping cannot change the stated nonlocality criterion, and the proposed SIN states do not exist under that criterion.
flags.evidence: Equation (8) assigns the right-identity case the entries beta_ix^2, beta_iy^2, beta_iz^2, and the following text claims this asymmetry furnishes swap-intolerant nonlocality. For a nonzero row v, beta^T beta = v^T v has eigenvalues {||v||^2, 0, 0}, exactly as in the nonzero-column case. More generally, swapping gives beta_prime = beta^T, and beta^T beta and beta beta^T have identical eigenvalues. Thus both label orders have M = beta_1^2 + beta_2^2 + beta_3^2; the second inequality in (9) does not make the swapped state local.

flags.location: Eigenvalue formulas (6) and (7), and the prescribed smallest eigenvalue in the proof of Theorem 1.4
flags.description: Both eigenvalue formulas omit the factor 1/4 required by the density-matrix definition. This also invalidates the claimed numerical value of the constructed smallest eigenvalue.
flags.evidence: Equation (1) defines rho = (I_4 + sum c_ij sigma_i tensor sigma_j)/4, but (6) and (7) report eigenvalues 1 +/- c_p +/- a square root. Their four eigenvalues sum to 4 rather than Tr(rho) = 1. With all coefficients zero they predict eigenvalues 1, whereas rho = I_4/4 has eigenvalues 1/4. In the theorem construction, taking tau_p = 0, E = (1 + |lambda_0|/2)e and C = -(|lambda_0|/2)e for a unit vector e satisfies the specified geometry but gives the actual minimum eigenvalue lambda_0/4.

flags.location: Proposition 2.1
flags.description: The two sphere assignments are reversed relative to the eigenvalues in (7), so the stated equivalence with positive semidefiniteness is false.
flags.evidence: The proposition places E in (C, r_+) and -E in (C, r_-). Equation (7), with E = (beta_i) and C = (tau_i), instead requires ||E + C|| <= 1 + tau_p and ||E - C|| <= 1 - tau_p, assigning -E to r_+ and E to r_-. For tau_p = 0.4, C = (0.2, 0, 0), E = (0.6, 0, 0), the actual normalized eigenvalues are {0.55, 0.15, 0.25, 0.05}, all positive, yet the proposition excludes the state because ||-E - C|| = 0.8 exceeds r_- = 0.6.

flags.location: Paragraph following Proposition 2.1
flags.description: Translating the coefficient-space points E and C does not generally preserve eigenvalues or positive semidefiniteness, because the reflected point must remain -E.
flags.evidence: The text claims that "under translations and rotations of the parameter space S, any eigenvalue-dependent property such as positive-definiteness is unchanged." Translating E and C by a preserves E - C but changes E + C to E + C + 2a, altering the first square root in (7). Starting with E = C = 0 and tau_p = 0 gives rho = I_4/4. Translating both by a = (1, 0, 0) produces normalized eigenvalues {3/4, -1/4, 1/4, 1/4}, destroying positive semidefiniteness.

flags.location: Concluding paragraph asserting coincident nonlocality and positivity boundaries
flags.description: The positive-semidefinite boundary is not generally the unit sphere in E-space; it also depends on the remaining coefficients. The manuscript therefore incorrectly identifies the two boundaries.
flags.evidence: The conclusion states that "the boundary for nonlocality in general in this case ... is the same as the boundary for positive semidefiniteness" and specifies |E| = 1. Holding C = 0 and tau_p = 0.8, equation (7) requires |E| <= 0.2 for positivity, whereas the rank-one correlation matrix gives M = |E|^2, crossing 1 at |E| = 1. For E = (0.3, 0, 0), the actual smallest eigenvalue is (1 - 0.8 - 0.3)/4 = -0.025 even though M = 0.09.

flags.evidence: The text introduces an arbitrary compact surface and states that its area remains 4π under ∂t g = 2(1−K)g. Differentiating area gives dArea/dt = 2Area−2∫K dV = 8π−4πχ(M) at Area = 4π, which need not vanish.

flags.location: Remark 2.2
flags.description: The displayed small-area expansion is algebraically false.
flags.evidence: The claimed equality is √(4πA−κA²) = √(4πA−κA³/(4√π)) + o(A²). The left expression is 2√π A^(1/2)−κ A^(3/2)/(4√π)+O(A^(5/2)); the right square root has no A^(3/2) term. Their difference is therefore not o(A²).

flags.location: Proposition 3.1, application of the maximum principle to the ODE solution
flags.description: The area-dependent ODE barrier is not a subsolution throughout the spatial domain, so the maximum principle does not establish the asserted bound with B(A).

flags.evidence: The proof asserts (4πA−κ(T)A²)/(4πA−A²) ≥ 1/(1+e^(−BT−C)). For fixed T>0 and κ(T)>1, its left side is 1−(κ(T)−1)A/(4π)+O(A²). rows.title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances

annotations.title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances
annotations.error_annotation: The error is the incorrect assumption in Sections 3 and 4 that the topology of the shortest path trees is public, which may not be true; additionally, in Section 3, Lemma 2.4 is applied inappropriately under this false assumption.

flags.location: Lemma 3.1, accuracy proof; Theorems 3.1 and 3.2
flags.description: The shortest noisy path is selected using the same noise whose concentration is being bounded, so its edge noises are not independent Laplace variables. In a chain of m diamonds, each with two disjoint two-edge branches of equal true weight, the 2m-hop estimate is a sum of m independent minima of two branch-noise sums. Each minimum has a negative mean of constant magnitude times 1/epsilon. Thus the error is Omega(m/epsilon) with high probability, contradicting O(sqrt(m) log(m)/epsilon) for n=3m+1. The advertised additive bounds rely on this false lemma.
flags.evidence: The proof states: "each distance ... is the sum of a maximum of t edge weights, hence the total error ... is the accumulation of at most t Laplace random variables," and then applies Lemma 2.4 and a union bound over n^2 distances.

flags.location: Theorem 4.3, privacy composition step; Appendix A, Corollary 4.1; analogous tree-based privacy claims in Sections 3 and 4
flags.description: The tree mechanism assumes fixed public topology, but these trees are selected from private weights. Its all-pairs output actually reveals tree structure through exact identities: for a tree containing the chain z-a-b, the released estimates satisfy d(z,b)=d(z,a)+d(a,b); for a tree with branches z-a and z-b they satisfy d(a,b)=d(z,a)+d(z,b). Changing only the triangle edge weight w(z,b) from M+1+eta to M+1-eta, with w(z,a)=M, w(a,b)=1 and 0<eta<=1/2, switches the shortest-path tree and these output supports. Consequently the claimed privacy of releasing all per-tree matrices does not follow from fixed-tree DP or composition, even if adjacency lists are hidden.
flags.evidence: Theorem 4.3 claims "By basic composition ... releasing all the private estimates is epsilon-DP." Appendix A computes each pair estimate using the lowest common ancestor and the identity d_T(x,y)=d(z,x)+d(z,y)-2d(z,v_x,y). Section 3 argues that not releasing shortest-path trees means "no shortest path information is revealed."

flags.location: Lemma 4.4 and its expectation bound in Construction 2
flags.description: The claimed cardinality lower bound can exceed the entire vertex set within the permitted parameter range. Take n=2^k and k=log_2(n)>=3. Then |A_1^r|=n/4 and t=ceil(200 log(n)), so Lemma 4.4 requires |A_1|>=tn/16>n. This event has probability zero. The proof incorrectly assumes |A_i^r|t<=n; uniform marginal inclusion also does not make the union size Binomial(n,p_i).
flags.evidence: Lemma 4.4 asserts "|A_i| >= (t/4) ... n^{1-(i+1)/k}" with probability at least 1-1/(2n^2). The proof uses "Let X_i ~ Binomial(n,p_i) be the number of vertices in A_i" and "the last inequality follows from |A_i^r| ... t <= n." The allowed range includes k=floor(log(n)/log(2)).

flags.location: Lemma 4.5, probability amplification in Construction 2
flags.description: The candidate comparisons share the same random second-nearest local center, so they cannot be amplified as independent events. For k=3, let q=n^{1/3}; A_1^r has q vertices and A_2 is the union of t independent singleton samples. On a star with distinct distances from its center u, take the first L=floor(n/(2t)) vertices in distance order. With constant probability every A_2 sample lies outside this prefix; conditional on that event, a fixed A_1^r contains at least two prefix vertices with probability Omega(q^2/t^2)=Omega(1/log^2(n)). Its second-nearest center then precedes all of A_2, violating the lemma. The failure probability is therefore much larger than 1/n^2.
flags.evidence: The proof asserts P[d(u,p_{i+1}(u)) <= d(u,A_i^r-{w})] >= 1-(1-1/(2|A_i^r|))^{|A_{i+1}|} >= 1-n^{-7}, then claims Lemma 4.5 holds with probability at least 1-1/n^2.

flags.location: Theorem 4.3, equation (3), and Theorem 4.4
flags.description: The accuracy calculation drops the log(n) factor in the number of trees. Corollary 4.1 with privacy budget epsilon/(tk) gives error O(tk log^{1.5}(n) log(ntk/gamma)/epsilon). Since t=ceil(100 n^{1/k} log(n)), equation (3) loses an additional log(n); its stated simplification should carry log^{3.5}(n) rather than log^{2.5}(n). Advanced composition analogously introduces sqrt(tk), so the approximate-DP calculation loses sqrt(log(n)). The displayed theorem bounds do not follow from the stated mechanism and corollary.
flags.evidence: Construction 2 defines t=ceil(100 n^{1/k} log(n)). Theorem 4.3 runs the "epsilon/(t ... k)-DP algorithm" but equation (3) bounds the error by O(k n^{1/k} log^{1.5}(n) log(n ... t ... k/gamma)/epsilon), omitting the log(n) factor contributed by t.

flags.description: The geometric-fiber condition in Definition 7 allows non-isotrivial infinitesimal deformations, contradicting the assertion that this category is a finite gerbe.
flags.evidence: Definition 7 requires only that every geometric fiber belong to xi. In characteristic zero, let xi=[x^2], S=Spec C[epsilon]/(epsilon^2), and psi(x)=x^2+epsilon on P^1_S. This satisfies the stated condition but is not an infinitesimal conjugate of x^2. For an infinitesimal Mobius transformation with vector field v=A+Bx+Cx^2, the change is 2xv(x)-v(x^2), whose constant and linear coefficients are -A and 2A; they cannot equal 1 and 0 simultaneously. A finite gerbe with the finite etale stabilizer of x^2 has no such deformation over this strictly local Artinian base.

annotations.error_annotation: The error is that the statements or proofs of Lemma 3 and Lemma 4 contain inaccuracies, likely due to incorrect assumptions, logical gaps, or invalid mathematical steps, which compromise the validity of their conclusions.

flags.location: Lemma 4, Eqs. (12)-(14), and Theorem 5
flags.description: The claimed partial-transpose gate has an invalid Gaussian-channel representation. For the supplied beam-splitter matrix, A = Z_2 B Z_2 gives q'_1 = (q_1 + q_2)/sqrt(2) and p'_1 = (p_1 - p_2)/sqrt(2), so [q'_1,p'_1] = 0 rather than i. It cannot implement a noiseless bosonic channel. Consequently, the zero-noise encoding and decoding assumed in Theorem 5 do not establish physical noise polarization. The operator-transpose identification also fails for the manuscript's single-mode squeezer: S-hat(r)^T = S-hat(-r), whereas Z S(r) Z = S(r).
flags.evidence: Lemma 4 assigns the partial transpose the matrices tilde M_i = Z_i M Z_i and tilde N_i = Z_i N Z_i. The text acknowledges that tilde M_i is generally nonsymplectic, although its earlier definition requires M to be symplectic for a noiseless Gaussian unitary. Theorem 5 nevertheless uses B_2(G^B) and B_2(G^(B^T)) as gates without added noise.

flags.location: Corollary 6 proof and Eq. (18)
flags.description: The proposed output drops the noise already present in the first shared pair. Even accepting Theorem 5 formally, applying the stated I_(1) tensor G_(2,3) to sigma_AB^(1) and the ancilla composes N^(e^(-2r) sigma^2) with the existing N^(sigma^2). Equation (3) makes their variances add, yielding (1 + e^(-2r)) sigma^2, rather than the reduced variance in Eq. (18). That equation would require an initially ideal first pair.
flags.evidence: Corollary 6 defines sigma_AB^(i) = (I_A tensor N_B^(sigma^2))(rho_zeta). Its proof encodes sigma_A^(1), and the preceding text explicitly says the composite channel acts on sigma_AB^(1) and rho_anc. Equation (18) then gives (I tensor N^(e^(-2r) sigma^2))(rho_zeta), omitting the initial N^(sigma^2).

flags.location: Appendix G, expansion of V and Eq. (G3)
flags.description: The fidelity expansion omits complex conjugation of the coefficients belonging to the adjoint operator. A checkable counterexample is W = exp(i pi n_j/2) tensor I_k with a vacuum ancilla. Because W is diagonal and the EPR components have equal occupation numbers, Psi_L = Psi_R for every finite r and tr(rho_0 V) = 1. The printed Eq. (G3), with two unconjugated alpha factors, instead gives (1 - tanh^2(r))/(1 + tanh^2(r)), tending to zero. The expression therefore cannot support the finite-squeezing fidelity claim.
flags.evidence: Appendix G defines V = (W^T_(i,k_1) tensor I_j)^dagger (I_i tensor W_(j,k_1)), but Eq. (G3) multiplies alpha_(n' m' n'' n_k_1) by alpha_(m' n' m_k_1 n'') with neither factor conjugated. The main text claims that the corresponding fidelity approaches 1 as r tends to infinity.
